questions.prompt: A function expects `{id: number}`. A variable has numeric id plus other fields. Why can it often be passed?

choices.text: The variable is automatically reconstructed as an instance of the expected interface.
Structural compatibility requires the expected members, not an exact nominal name.
All object arguments are accepted because TypeScript ignores required properties.
Extra fields are erased from the object before the call is executed.

questions.explanation: Structural typing compares required shape. A compatible variable can have additional fields; those fields are not removed at runtime.

questions.prompt: A fresh object literal passed to `{color?: string}` includes a misspelled `colour` property. Why can the compiler reject it?

choices.text: Fresh object literals receive excess property checks for likely mistakes.
Every structurally typed object must have exactly one property at runtime.
Optional properties forbid passing any object literal to the function.
The compiler translates colour into color and reports the successful conversion.

questions.explanation: Excess property checking catches suspicious extra fields on fresh literals. It is a static check, not runtime rewriting or a ban on optional properties.

questions.prompt: An object is viewed through a readonly property type while another alias remains mutable. What can happen?

choices.text: The readonly view freezes the object for all existing aliases at runtime.
TypeScript clones the object so aliases can no longer share its properties.
The mutable alias becomes readonly automatically in every calling module.
The mutable alias can still change the underlying object.

questions.explanation: Readonly restricts assignments through that static view. It is not a runtime freeze and does not eliminate mutable aliases.

questions.prompt: A generic identity function returns its argument. Why use `<T>(value:T):T` instead of any?

choices.text: It validates arbitrary JSON against T before returning the argument.
It forces every caller to pass the same globally fixed concrete type.
It preserves the caller specific input type in the return relationship.
It deep-clones the argument so the input and output never share identity.

questions.explanation: The type parameter relates the argument and return type for each call. Any loses that relationship; generics do not clone or validate data.

sources.title: TypeScript: Generics
sources.claim: Generics preserve relationships between input and output types, and constraints restrict supported operations without discarding the type parameter.

questions.prompt: Two interfaces have the same required public members but different names. What usually determines assignment compatibility?

choices.text: The runtime constructor identity automatically generated for both interfaces.
Their required structural members rather than the interface names alone.
The lexical order of their declarations regardless of member types.
Only their interface names, even when all public members match.

questions.explanation: Interfaces are generally structural and do not emit runtime constructors. Member shape matters rather than the chosen interface names alone.

questions.prompt: An API intentionally accepts arbitrary string keys with numeric values. Which type feature expresses that contract?

choices.text: A string index signature with a numeric value type.
An excess-property suppression that changes every runtime value to a number.
A readonly property that allows any name and any value without checking.
A generic parameter with no constraint that guarantees numeric property values.

questions.explanation: An index signature specifies allowed indexed keys and their value type. It expresses a deliberate open-object shape rather than disabling value checking.

questions.prompt: A team reviews structural object contracts. Which claims hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Declaring an interface creates a runtime constructor.
Required member types affect compatibility.
Compatible variables can include additional members.
Interface names alone always enforce nominal identity.
Assigning a variable to a narrower view erases its extra runtime fields.

questions.explanation: a: Interfaces describe types without emitting a constructor. b: Having a member with the wrong type is not enough. c: Structural compatibility need not require an exact property set. d: Interfaces are generally compared structurally. e: Static assignment does not transform the object.

questions.prompt: A fresh literal fails an excess property check. Which conclusions hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: The check can detect a misspelled option name.
An index signature can model intentionally open keys.
An assertion can affect checking without rewriting the object.
Every variable with extra compatible fields must fail the same check.
The compiler silently deletes excess fields from emitted objects.

questions.explanation: a: It targets likely mistakes in fresh literals. b: It declares accepted indexed properties. c: Assertions are static and do not rename fields. d: Fresh-literal excess checks are stricter than ordinary variable compatibility. e: The check is not runtime field removal.

questions.prompt: A readonly interface exposes shared mutable state. Which claims hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Another mutable alias can still modify the object.
Readonly implies a deep runtime Object.freeze operation.
All nested objects become deeply immutable automatically.
The compiler creates separate objects for readonly and mutable views.
Readonly prevents assignment through that typed property.

questions.explanation: a: Readonly does not guarantee absence of aliases. b: The type modifier emits no such operation. c: Readonly properties can still reference mutable nested objects. d: The static views may refer to the same runtime object. e: It restricts use of the readonly view.

questions.prompt: A generic helper reads keys from objects. Which contracts hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: K extends keyof T limits K to keys of T.
Using any preserves all caller-specific relationships automatically.
A generic constraint inserts runtime validation code.
A type parameter can preserve an input-output relationship.
A constraint permits operations supported by the constrained shape.

questions.explanation: a: That constraint relates the key parameter to the object type. b: Any bypasses the relation the generic parameter can express. c: It is a static restriction on acceptable typed use. d: The return can be expressed using the same T. e: The checker knows those members exist.
